items.misconception: Accusative (because it sounds like a direct relationship).
items.why: Students guess case based on logic. Mit is a DATIVE preposition - one of several you memorise (aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu - mnemonic). Each preposition has a fixed case.

items.q: Which relative pronoun do you use for 'the man WHOM I saw' in German?
items.why: Students don't decline relative pronouns. The relative pronoun takes the case its FUNCTION REQUIRES in its clause. 'Whom I saw' makes it the direct object, so accusative: 'Der Mann, DEN ich gesehen habe.'

items.q: How do you say 'I'm travelling to Germany' in German?
items.why: Students use 'in' or 'zu'. For most countries and cities: NACH (Deutschland, Berlin, Paris). For countries with articles (die Schweiz, die USA): IN with accusative. Easy to mix up - nach is for proper place names without articles.

items.q: Which sentence correctly says 'I get on well with my mother'?
items.correct: Ich verstehe mich gut mit meiner Mutter.
items.misconception: Ich verstehe mich gut mit meine Mutter.
items.random_wrong: Ich verstehe mir gut mit meiner Mutter.
items.why: Correct answer: Ich verstehe mich gut mit meiner Mutter.. “Ich verstehe mich gut mit meine Mutter.” sounds right because it borrows the language of the topic — but it fails this question. Re-read the notes on why.

items.q: Which form of 'you' do you use addressing a German teacher?
items.why: Correct answer: Sie. “du” sounds right because it borrows the language of the topic — but it fails this question. Re-read the notes on why.

items.q: How many grammatical cases does standard German have?
items.why: The real figure is 4 cases. The wrong options cluster deliberately close — anchor the exact number to one concrete fact so it can't drift.
